label: Place
name: Equatorial Guinea
summary:
Equatorial Guinea, officially the Republic of Equatorial Guinea, is a country on the west coast of Central Africa comprising a mainland section (Río Muni) bordering Cameroon and Gabon, and several islands including Bioko (where the capital Malabo is located). With 1.5 million people, it is Africa's smallest mainland country by population and the only sovereign African state where Spanish is an official language.

Formerly the Spanish colony of Spanish Guinea, Equatorial Guinea gained independence in 1968. The dictatorship of Francisco Macías Nguema (1968–1979) was one of the most brutal in African history — a cult-of-personality tyranny that killed or drove into exile an estimated third of the population and was dubbed 'the Auschwitz of Africa' by observers. He was overthrown in a coup by his nephew Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo in 1979.

The discovery of offshore oil (1995) transformed Equatorial Guinea from one of Africa's poorest countries into one of its highest GDP-per-capita states — but wealth has been spectacularly concentrated in the Obiang family, with the population remaining among Africa's most impoverished by most social indicators. Obiang's son Teodorin Nguema became internationally notorious for spending oil revenues on luxury yachts, private jets, and Malibu mansions while serving as agriculture minister. The country represents one of the starkest examples in the world of resource wealth captured by a ruling family with virtually no benefit to the population.

This event has had a lasting impact on regional politics and human rights discourse.
